item.title: Oil Price Today (November 25): Brent crude dips below $91 as traders weigh new attacks, rising supply. What are experts saying?
item.description: Crude oil price : Oil prices have dipped slightly due to an uptick in supply and renewed threats against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Exports from the Gulf have surged, resulting in notable price volatility. Analysts are wary of impending geopolitical tensions, predicting an escalation in prices should conflicts persist. Major financial institutions like Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan have adjusted their forecasts amid this uncertainty, making long-term oil market predictions increasingly complex.
item.dc:creator: Veer Sharma
item.content:encoded: Oil prices edged lower in early Asian trade on Wednesday, November 25, as traders weighed rising supply against a fresh series of attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.Iran's Fars news agency reported on Tuesday that a fourth tanker had been hit by a mine, adding to a series of recent attacks on vessels targeted by Tehran. Iran also plans to tighten its control over the Strait of Hormuz until its demands are met, according to a report by the country's Tasnim News agency. The developments underline how far the nearly nine-month conflict remains from a resolution.ALSO READ:D-Street poised for a gap-up start as GIFT Nifty trades firmly higherCrude oil price on November 25Brent crude slipped to $90.96 or down 0.5% a barrel after settling above $91 on Monday. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures for January delivery fell 0.62% to $81.54, extending losses after gaining 2.4% in the previous session.However, crude exports from the Gulf region have increased sharply in recent months, while the International Energy Agency expects the oil market to move into a surplus this quarter. Brent has fallen significantly this month, partly after US President Donald Trump refrained from launching fresh strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections.On the diplomatic front, US Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio held separate meetings with Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani on Monday, according to an AP report. Qatar has been instrumental in efforts to restart stalled negotiations aimed at ending the conflict.Meanwhile, attacks on shipping continued. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a container ship had been targeted while travelling along what they described as an unauthorised route near the Strait of Hormuz, according to state media. Separately, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said on Tuesday that three vessels were hit by unidentified projectiles on Monday while sailing east through the strait.ALSO READ: Stocks in news: Adani Enterprises, Tata Steel, PhysicsWallah, Hyundai Motor India, Lenskart and HindalcoWhere are prices headed?The recent weakness in oil prices comes against the backdrop of longer-term supply risks highlighted by Goldman Sachs. Earlier this month, the bank raised its oil price projections, warning that Brent crude could reach $140 a barrel in 2027 if Gulf oil production remains substantially below its 2025 average.Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $105 a barrel from $90 previously. Its forecast for WTI was increased to $94 from $81.In a more bullish scenario, Brent could climb to $140 a barrel and average around $130 in 2027 if Gulf oil production stays 3.5 million barrels per day below its 2025 average, Reuters reported, citing the bank's projections.The bank expects geopolitical uncertainty to add a greater risk premium to oil prices. Its assessment factors in the possibility of further disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies, the historical duration of major supply shocks and the difficulties involved in securing a lasting diplomatic settlement.These projections reflect the extent to which the longer-term outlook for crude remains dependent on developments in the conflict, even as expectations of stronger exports continue to weigh on prices in the near term.JPMorgan analysts have also warned that the conflict remains unpredictable, making its potential consequences difficult to gauge. The bank had initially expected the US administration to avoid crossing certain economic thresholds. However, seven months into the conflict, several of those thresholds have been crossed, with no clear strategy yet in place to end the war.According to the brokerage, oil markets will continue to face competing pressures from the possibility of supply disruptions and the industry's capacity to respond to them.JPMorgan's base-case scenario assumes that Middle Eastern oil supplies will remain above their 2025 average, supported by measures such as ship-to-ship transfers and additional pipeline capacity. At the same time, production growth in other regions is expected to come to a halt.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. item.title: Dollar takes breather ahead of US data on Fed path; Aussie jumps on CPI
item.description: The US dollar remained steady as traders awaited important inflation and growth data prior to December. Economists expect the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, which is currently predicted at 97%. In Japan, service-sector prices surged to a 36-year high, while the Australian dollar rose after inflation data exceeded forecasts. Concerns about the sustainability of the AI market have impacted investor sentiment.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The US dollar took a breather on Wednesday ahead of inflation and growth data, the last major readings before a December Federal Reserve policy meeting at which traders see a 97% chance of an interest rate hike.The yen held steady following figures showing Japan's service-sector prices jumped to a 36-year high in October. The Australian dollar climbed after data showing hotter-than-forecast inflation in October.Investor attention now turns to the release of US gross domestic product data for the third quarter as well as the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. The greenback gave up ground on Tuesday as concern crept back into the AI trade that has attracted vast sums of capital to the US. The whole of November has been a really, really strong month for the US dollar, Rodrigo Catril, a senior FX strategist at the National Australia Bank, said on a podcast. So it's a little bit of a consolidation story in currencies rather than safe haven for the US dollar as the theme. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against six peers, was flat at 103.85 following a 0.44% slide in the prior session. The euro was down 0.03% at $1.0961.The yen edged 0.03% lower to 159.28 a dollar, while sterling weakened 0.05% to $1.3106.With no end in sight to the Middle East crisis, elevated oil prices have kept central banks in a hawkish posture to rein in inflation. Euro zone policymaker Olaf Sleijpen said on Tuesday the European Central Bank is likely to raise its policy interest rate in December, though the path after that is unclear.Fed funds futures traders are pricing in 97% odds of a Fed hike in December, and a 66% chance of an additional increase in January, showed the CME Group's FedWatch Tool. But with concern about the viability of the AI trade driving recent share selling, investors have begun to question how much the Fed can tighten policy without crimping the economy.On Wednesday, the US Commerce Department is widely expected to report that the Personal Consumption Expenditures index nudged up 0.3% in October, compared with a 0.5% gain in the month before. The agency will also release its second estimate of GDP for the third quarter, which market participants expect to show that the economy grew at a 3.5% annualised rate.In Japan, a key gauge of service-sector inflation jumped 4.2% in October from a year earlier, official data showed on Wednesday, a sign of broadening price pressure that bolsters the case for a near-term interest rate hike by the central bank.Data also on Wednesday showed Australian consumer prices climbed by more than markets expected in October, while a stubbornly high reading for core inflation underlined why the policy interest rate has risen five times this year.The Australian dollar strengthened 0.29% versus the greenback to $0.6657, while New Zealand's kiwi weakened 0.09% to $0.5477.In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin fell 0.52% to $59,507.77, while ether declined 0.54% to $1,669.73.

item.title: Global Market Today: Asian stocks fall as AI trade doubts resurface
item.description: The MSCI Asia Pacific Index slipped 0.6%, losing ground after posting its biggest rally since July on Tuesday. The losses were led by South Korea’s Kospi index, which declined 3.7%.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Asian stocks retreated, tracking losses on Wall Street, after a renewed selloff in US technology stocks revived doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade.The MSCI Asia Pacific Index slipped 0.6%, losing ground after posting its biggest rally since July on Tuesday. The losses were led by South Korea’s Kospi index, which declined 3.7%.As sentiment weakened, US equity-index futures fell in early Asian trading. Earlier, the Nasdaq 100 Index lost 2% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index tumbled 7.9%, taking its decline from a June peak to 40%. Nvidia sank 5.9%, while Anthropic PBC traded below its IPO price. Shares of Dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. rose in extended trading after they issued upbeat forecasts.Read more: Stocks in news: Adani Enterprises, Tata Steel, PhysicsWallah, Hyundai Motor India, Lenskart and HindalcoElsewhere, Treasuries rose in the New York session on haven demand, while the dollar weakened. Oil edged higher on Monday as tanker attacks overshadowed diplomatic efforts to resolve the US-Iran war. Gold fell and copper closed at a 13-month low in New York.The sharp swings underscore the uncertainty surrounding the AI trade as investors question whether massive technology spending can deliver enough growth to justify elevated valuations. Traders are also parsing the Trump administration’s push to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court. The US is set to announce as soon as Tuesday plans to raise tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and more than a dozen other economies, according to people familiar with the matter.“This is so dizzying day to day,” said Adam Phillips, managing director of portfolio strategy at EP Wealth Advisors, who is not buying the dip in stocks yet. “Nothing has significantly changed from Monday, but we’re not out of the woods yet. There is still a whole lot of fear and uncertainty around the AI trade that needs to be worked through.”Traders face several key risk events on Wednesday, including a US inflation reading and the possible tariff announcement from the Trump administration.The additional tariffs won’t push overall rates above levels agreed in individual trade deals, including pacts President Donald Trump negotiated with the EU and China, people familiar with the details said. Still, the renewed focus on tariffs revived concerns about the potential impact on economic growth, corporate profits and inflation.“The last thing Wall Street wants to hear right now is anything about a trade war in the midst of all the AI uncertainty,” said Charles Lemonides, principal and portfolio manager of ValueWorks LLC. “Any reports perceived as a potential negative for the economy or corporate earnings will spook investors.”Investors also weighed fresh economic data showing inflation concerns have yet to curb spending ahead of the holiday-shopping season, with US consumer confidence surging to the highest in nearly two years.The report came on the eve of the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation metric, which is seen adding to bets that officials will raise interest rates in December.Even as the Fed tightens policy, Treasuries will continue to advance over the next year, according to Joe Maher at Capital Economics.“That’s because we think the tech-driven rout in the stock market has further to run and will prompt investors to revise down their rate expectations and trigger a ‘flight-to-safety’ into bonds,” he said.
